transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I’m so preoccupied with how awful my face and neck look now that I’m starting to avoid the very community things that used to keep me going. I just feel so self-conscious about how much I've aged that it's getting hard to face people.
Are you avoiding social situations because you're afraid of being judged or embarrassed, or is it mainly because you feel your appearance doesn't meet your standards?

It’s really about how intolerable I find my own appearance. I feel like my face and neck look completely deformed and disfigured by all the sagging skin and deep wrinkles. Even though people tell me I look fine, I just can't stand the thought of being up there in front of everyone or in photos looking so awful.
How much time do you spend each day thinking about or checking your appearance, such as in mirrors or photos?

I spend a really disruptive amount of time on it, especially before my workshops or choir practice. I get stuck in the bathroom mirror for ages adjusting my scarf and makeup, leaning in and out, and taking my glasses on and off to check my neck and jaw. I even end up taking a bunch of selfies on my phone just to zoom in and inspect every single wrinkle.
When you look in the mirror and see your face and neck as deformed or disfigured, do you believe that what you're seeing is accurate, even though others tell you otherwise?

Yes, it feels completely real and undeniable to me; when I look in the mirror, I truly see a deformed neck and face. Even though a part of me knows people say I look fine for my age, I just can't help but believe my own eyes. That's why it causes me so much distress and why I decided to seek help.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F45.2", "F63.3"], but based on this conversation, F45.2 (hypochondriacal disorder) seems unlikely because the patient's preoccupation is specifically with their appearance—particularly facial and neck aging—and not with having a medical illness such as cancer or heart disease. The patient experiences a distressing, persistent belief that their appearance is deformed despite others' reassurance, spends excessive time checking in mirrors and photos, and avoids social activities due to appearance-related distress. These features strongly support F63.3 (body dysmorphic disorder), where the core pathology is a preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance. The conviction in the perceived flaw being real, even with partial insight, aligns with ICD-10 criteria for F63.3.
